messages.subject: Creating density surface and estimating regional population size from averaged models?
messages.subject_clean: Creating density surface and estimating regional population size from averaged models?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have narrowed down my models using AICc. The top models (dAIC <2 or <4 or <7) are all very similar but I'm not convinced any single model is best to calculate density surfaces (predictDsurface or fx.total) or regional population sizes (regoin.N) from.

Is there a way to model average my best models then estimate density surfaces and regional population sizes from model-averaged parameters?

Something like this?

BestModels <- model.average(model1, model2, ..., model100, dmax=4)

BestModelSurface<- predictDsurface(BestModels)
BestModelDSUM <- fx.total(BestModels)

region.N(BestModels, region=Region1Mask)

Obviously this doesn't work, but this is my train of thought.

Thank.

messages.subject: Re: Creating density surface and estimating regional population size from averaged models?
messages.subject_clean: Creating density surface and estimating regional population size from averaged models?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kyle

First, let's get rid of the idea that fx.total generates density surfaces - it doesn't. You get a coloured picture with interesting bumps. The width of the bumps depends on how much sampling you do. The number and location of the bumps depends on which individuals actually got detected your particular trial. The lack of relief towards the edges reflects the increasing dominance of the model over the sample. This is not a density surface.

Your general question is not unreasonable. The short answer is 'No, you can't do that in secr'.

A slightly longer answer might be: You envisage a single model called 'BestModels' whose predictions are the same as model-averaged estimates from several models. I can see this working for averaging on the link (beta) scale (with some headaches over variances - maybe someone would want to program this), but not on the response (real) scale.

It is quite feasible to apply predictDsurface to each model in turn and to form a weighted sum of the cell-specific predicted densities. I think this might do it:
averageDsurface <- function (modellist, mask, criterion = 'AICc') {
  wt <- paste0(criterion, "wt")
  wts <- AIC(modellist, criterion = criterion)[,wt]
  surfaces <- lapply(modellist, predictDsurface, mask = mask)
  D0mat <- sapply(surfaces, function(x) covariates(x)$D.0)
  D0mat <- sweep(D0mat, MARGIN = 2, STATS = wts, FUN = "*")
  outsurface <- surfaces[[1]]
  covariates(outsurface) <- data.frame(D.0 = apply(D0mat,1,sum))
  outsurface
}
## for example
possummodels <- secrlist(possum.model.0, possum.model.Ds) # or output from par.secr.fit
averagedD <- averageDsurface(possummodels, possummask)
plot(averagedD)

You're on your own for SE.

It's not clear whether you have different density surface models or different detection models (or maybe both). My own feeling (you didn't ask for this, but here it is...) is that model averaging different density surfaces will just cloud interpretation, and model averaging detection models usually has trivial effects, so why bother?

messages.subject: Questions re understanding the effective sampling area (esa) in package ‘secr’
messages.subject_clean: Questions re understanding the effective sampling area (esa) in package ‘secr’
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I’m new to SECR modelling, and am trying to understand how effective sampling areas (esa) are calculated. Many thanks in advance for any insights you can provide! I’ve tried to explain my current level of understanding below, and have highlighted questions in bold.

>From the Borchers and Efford 2008 paper, it seems that in the simple case where density (D) is constant and there are no covariates, the esa for each trap is the integral of the capture function (i.e. the equation for 'a' on page 379). Am I understanding that correctly?

Using the example hare dataset available in package ‘secr’ and leveraging the corresponding tutorial example, I wrote the following R code to calculate the integral of a half-normal capture function:

hareCH6 <- read.capthist("Data/hareCH6capt.txt", "Data/hareCH6trap.txt", detector = "single")

initialsigma <- RPSV(hareCH6, CC = TRUE)

fit.HN <- secr.fit (hareCH6, buffer = 4 * initialsigma, detectfn = 'HN', trace = FALSE)

logit2prob <- function(logit){ # from https://sebastiansauer.github.io/convert_logit2prob/

  odds <- exp(logit)

  prob <- odds / (1 + odds)

  return(prob)

}

g0_logit <- coef(fit.HN)$beta[2]

g0_prob <- logit2prob(g0_logit)

sigma_log <- coef(fit.HN)$beta[3]

sigma_prob <- exp(sigma_log)

d <- seq(from = 0, to = 200, by = 1) # distance in m

capture_function <- function(d){

  P <- g0_prob*exp(-(d^2)/(2*sigma_prob^2)) # see page 49 of the secr manual for this formula

  return(P)

}

plot(d, capture_function(d)) # graph of the function as calculated by me above

plot(fit.HN, xval = 0:200) # graph of the function as generated automatically - good news, they match!

area_under_capture_function_curve_m2 <- integrate(capture_function, lower = 0, upper = Inf)

For the example hare dataset, this gives me: area_under_capture_function_curve_m2 =  5.275324 with absolute error < 4.6e-06.

I also noticed that the package ‘secr’ can calculate the esa directly, but presumably this is the esa for the entire trapping area (not just one trap). Am I correct in thinking that the esa calculated by the R package ‘secr’ is for the entire trapping area?

Again using the example hare dataset, I wrote the following R code to estimate the entire trapping area:

esa_all_traps_hectares <- derived(fit.HN)$estimate[1]

This gives me an esa of 46.38597 hectares.

How does this esa for the entire trapping area work, and how is it related to the ‘area under the capture function curve’ approach (i.e. where I got ~5m2 for each trap)?

On a separate but related note, would it be appropriate to look at the capture function curve and take the distance that corresponds with 95% of the area under the curve as an estimate of the radius of the effective sampling area for each trap assuming it is a circle?

A huge thanks again in advance for your help!

Much appreciated,

Laura

messages.subject_clean: Questions re understanding the effective sampling area (esa) in package ‘secr’
messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura
I think you're integrating the wrong fn. You want what 'secr' calls pdot (x) - the probability that an animal at x is detected by at least one detector. See ?pdot; summing pdot values and scaling by cell size gives you esa. Note D-hat = n/esa where n is number of different individuals.
Murray

P.S. try ?invlogit

Sent from my Samsung Galaxy smartphone.

messages.subject: Re: Questions re understanding the effective sampling area (esa) in package ‘secr’
messages.subject_clean: Questions re understanding the effective sampling area (esa) in package ‘secr’
messages.body_plain:
To answer your questions in bold:

(1) The equation for 'a' on page 379 is the integral of the capture function, but note that it is the integral for the combined capture function of all traps over all occasions. A per-trap esa could be obtained by integrating the capture function for a single trap (combined over all occasions), as I think you suggest. If you integrated the capture function for a single occasion, you'd get an "esa" for a single trap on a single occasion, not for a single trap over the whole survey (unless the survey involved only one occasion - and I think you do have only one occasion, and that this is what you have done).

(2) Yes, you are correct in thinking that "the esa calculated by the R package ‘secr’ is for the entire trapping area" - presuming that you mean "for all traps combined" when you say "for the entire trapping area".

(3) How does this esa for the entire trapping area work, and how is it related to the ‘area under the capture function curve’ approach (i.e. where I got ~5m2 for each trap)?

The esa for all traps combined is as per the equation for a on page 379, where the integrand is what secr calls pdot(x), which is given by the equation on the second line of page 379.

Assuming that there is only one occasion, the relationship between this a and the per-trap esa is just that the esa for all traps combined integrates over {1 - product_k [1-p_k(x)]} (i.e. the probability that at least one trap detects an animal with activity centre at x) whereas the per-trap esa integrates over p_k(x) (i.e. the probability that the kth trap detects an animal with activity centre at x).

(4) On a separate but related note, would it be appropriate to look at the capture function curve and take the distance that corresponds with 95% of the area under the curve as an estimate of the radius of the effective sampling area for each trap assuming it is a circle?

No, that is not correct. The detection function is not a probability density function. But it is easy to calculate what I think you might want: the "effective radius" of a single trap would be the square root of [the per-trap esa divided by pi] (from the formula for the area of a circle: a = pi*r^2). This gives the radius within which you would expect to make as many detections as expected from your detection function, if you detected everything with activity centres within this radius and nothing beyond it. (I don't know if you were thinking this, but advise you to avoid the temptation to think in terms of some fixed radius within which you detect stuff and beyond which you don't - that is not the way that the detection process works.)

Finally, note that all of the above refers to the case in which density is assumed constant. The concept of an esa falls apart a bit when you have non-uniform density. (You can generalise it for that case, but its interpretation is then not as intuitive.)

Hi Laura

I think you're integrating the wrong fn. You want what 'secr' calls pdot (x) - the probability that an animal at x is detected by at least one detector. See ?pdot; summing pdot values and scaling by cell size gives you esa. Note D-hat = n/esa where n is number of different individuals.

Hello,

I’m new to SECR modelling, and am trying to understand how effective sampling areas (esa) are calculated. Many thanks in advance for any insights you can provide! I’ve tried to explain my current level of understanding below, and have highlighted questions in bold.

>From the Borchers and Efford 2008 paper, it seems that in the simple case where density (D) is constant and there are no covariates, the esa for each trap is the integral of the capture function (i.e. the equation for 'a' on page 379). Am I understanding that correctly?

Using the example hare dataset available in package ‘secr’ and leveraging the corresponding tutorial example, I wrote the following R code to calculate the integral of a half-normal capture function:

hareCH6 <- read.capthist("Data/hareCH6capt.txt", "Data/hareCH6trap.txt", detector = "single")

initialsigma <- RPSV(hareCH6, CC = TRUE)

fit.HN <- secr.fit (hareCH6, buffer = 4 * initialsigma, detectfn = 'HN', trace = FALSE)

logit2prob <- function(logit){ # from https://sebastiansauer.github.io/convert_logit2prob/

  odds <- exp(logit)

  prob <- odds / (1 + odds)

  return(prob)

}

g0_logit <- coef(fit.HN)$beta[2]

g0_prob <- logit2prob(g0_logit)

sigma_log <- coef(fit.HN)$beta[3]

sigma_prob <- exp(sigma_log)

d <- seq(from = 0, to = 200, by = 1) # distance in m

capture_function <- function(d){

  P <- g0_prob*exp(-(d^2)/(2*sigma_prob^2)) # see page 49 of the secr manual for this formula

  return(P)

}

plot(d, capture_function(d)) # graph of the function as calculated by me above

plot(fit.HN, xval = 0:200) # graph of the function as generated automatically - good news, they match!

area_under_capture_function_curve_m2 <- integrate(capture_function, lower = 0, upper = Inf)

Again using the example hare dataset, I wrote the following R code to estimate the entire trapping area:

esa_all_traps_hectares <- derived(fit.HN)$estimate[1]

This gives me an esa of 46.38597 hectares.

How does this esa for the entire trapping area work, and how is it related to the ‘area under the capture function curve’ approach (i.e. where I got ~5m2 for each trap)?

On a separate but related note, would it be appropriate to look at the capture function curve and take the distance that corresponds with 95% of the area under the curve as an estimate of the radius of the effective sampling area for each trap assuming it is a circle?

A huge thanks again in advance for your help!

Much appreciated,

Laura

From: secr...@googlegroups.com [mailto:secr...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of David Borchers
Sent: Friday, July 21, 2017 7:58 AM
To: secr <secr...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: Questions re understanding the effective sampling area (esa) in package ‘secr’

To answer your questions in bold:

(1) The equation for 'a' on page 379 is the integral of the capture function, but note that it is the integral for the combined capture function of all traps over all occasions. A per-trap esa could be obtained by integrating the capture function for a single trap (combined over all occasions), as I think you suggest. If you integrated the capture function for a single occasion, you'd get an "esa" for a single trap on a single occasion, not for a single trap over the whole survey (unless the survey involved only one occasion - and I think you do have only one occasion, and that this is what you have done).

(2) Yes, you are correct in thinking that "the esa calculated by the R package ‘secr’ is for the entire trapping area" - presuming that you mean "for all traps combined" when you say "for the entire trapping area".

(3) How does this esa for the entire trapping area work, and how is it related to the ‘area under the capture function curve’ approach (i.e. where I got ~5m2 for each trap)?

The esa for all traps combined is as per the equation for a on page 379, where the integrand is what secr calls pdot(x), which is given by the equation on the second line of page 379.

Assuming that there is only one occasion, the relationship between this a and the per-trap esa is just that the esa for all traps combined integrates over {1 - product_k [1-p_k(x)]} (i.e. the probability that at least one trap detects an animal with activity centre at x) whereas the per-trap esa integrates over p_k(x) (i.e. the probability that the kth trap detects an animal with activity centre at x).

(4) On a separate but related note, would it be appropriate to look at the capture function curve and take the distance that corresponds with 95% of the area under the curve as an estimate of the radius of the effective sampling area for each trap assuming it is a circle?

No, that is not correct. The detection function is not a probability density function. But it is easy to calculate what I think you might want: the "effective radius" of a single trap would be the square root of [the per-trap esa divided by pi] (from the formula for the area of a circle: a = pi*r^2). This gives the radius within which you would expect to make as many detections as expected from your detection function, if you detected everything with activity centres within this radius and nothing beyond it. (I don't know if you were thinking this, but advise you to avoid the temptation to think in terms of some fixed radius within which you detect stuff and beyond which you don't - that is not the way that the detection process works.)

Finally, note that all of the above refers to the case in which density is assumed constant. The concept of an esa falls apart a bit when you have non-uniform density. (You can generalise it for that case, but its interpretation is then not as intuitive.)

messages.body_plain: I'm interested if my organisms are moving in certain directions across the landscape. Is there a function in package secr that estimates the average direction of subsequent spatial recaptures?

messages.subject_clean: Any function in package secr that estimates the average direction of subsequent spatial recaptures?
messages.body_plain:
It might help if we had a better understanding of the process of directional movement you have in mind.  Do you think activity centers move directionally across occasions?  If so, you could perhaps modify the markov movement model of Royle et al. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10144-015-0524-z) to have directional movement.  If you think animal movement is elongated along a major axis and reduced along a minor axis around fixed activity centers, you could perhaps try the anisotropic detection functions I used in this paper (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jwmg.21144/full) to infer bears preferentially moved along linear ridges.  It has code to implement in secr.  In the first model, the order of the detections would matter while in the second model, the order does not.  Or maybe you have something else in mind.

messages.body_plain:
The format used will become the units of distance inference, and hence it overwhelmingly makes sense to use Northing and Easting in metres (and Mercator distortion is unlikely to be an issue at most study scales).

Any GIS software will be able to convert easily among them, but there are also online converters e.g. LINZ.

James

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am having a problem believing the results that I am getting from secr. Can anybody advise me whether there’s a mistake in my secr code below.

I used spatial explicit capture-recapture analyses with secr to estimate density of a giant carnivorous land snail in a 70 m square plot.

The density estimate obtained using this code  was implausible: 30% higher than from MARK. – Estimates from secr should be lower because MARK population estimates are inflated by the influence of snails with home-ranges straddling the plot boundary.

I used home range estimates from concurrent radio-tracking to generate simulated population distributions and tested secr performance with the simulations.

Density estimates from secr were 45% higher than the simulated population densities.

 The mark-recapture period lasted 20 days with 5 capture occasions.The  buffer value of 4  is based on my radio-tracking data.

There was close to zero probability of snails with home-range centers >4 m outside of the plot entering the plot during the capture-recapture period.
